Trade META on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), the social-media and advertising giant, drew investor interest Monday as the market reassessed the pace of AI development, according to Barron's. The picture puts shares at $655. A slower AI race could take some pressure off spending, but investors should keep that possibility separate from an actual budget cut.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 2 Warning Sign with META.

Is META fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

META GF Value chart

The latest quarterly numbers show why spending matters. Meta's second-quarter revenue climbed 28% to $60.80 billion, but costs and expenses jumped 55% to $42.03 billion. Operating income dropped 8%. Operating margin slid to 31% from 43%, surrendering 12 percentage points despite strong sales growth. The advertising business is expanding. Expenses are expanding much faster.

Meta Gains - But Its 12-Point Margin Slide Still Demands Answers · us.finance.gurufocus

The picture places Meta 23.16% below its $852.42 GF Value estimate, suggesting potential undervaluation rather than guaranteeing upside. That discount needs an earnings argument behind it. Stronger advertising demand alone has not stopped margin erosion, and a cooler AI race would not automatically reverse it. For investors, the next test is whether Meta can bring expense growth back below revenue growth and turn more of those additional sales into operating profit.

title: AI-Related Debt Sales Are Near $500 Billion. Meta and CoreWeave Show Why the Same Boom Creates Two Different Risks
detail:
AI-Related Debt Sales Are Near $500 Billion. Meta and CoreWeave Show Why the Same Boom Creates Two Different Risks
Habib Ur Rehman
Mon, September 14, 2026 at 2:02 PM CDT 3 min read
CRWV
META
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

AI infrastructure is becoming a credit story as much as a technology story. Reuters Breakingviews reported that AI-related debt issuance had reached nearly $500 billion by early August, about one-fifth of higher-rated U.S. issuance this year versus roughly 1% in 2024.

Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and CoreWeave, Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) sit at opposite ends of that financing spectrum. Both need staggering amounts of compute. Only one can fund most mistakes from a giant advertising machine.

Meta can borrow against cash flow. CoreWeave borrows against the build

Meta's advantage is balance-sheet depth. Its advertising business can support AI capex before every new data center proves its individual return. Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META) also benefits if lenders increasingly demand guarantees, signed leases and stronger counterparties, because weaker projects become harder to finance.

AI-Related Debt Sales Are Near $500 Billion. Meta and CoreWeave Show Why the Same Boom Creates Two Different Risks

Affordability does not remove the capital-discipline problem. Meta can afford spending that still destroys value. If AI infrastructure keeps consuming cash faster than new products improve advertising, engagement or monetization, shareholders absorb lower returns even without a solvency problem.

CoreWeave's model is more sensitive to financing conditions. CoreWeave, Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) ended Q2 with about $104 billion of backlog, which supports the case that infrastructure is being built against real demand. It also spent $9.4 billion on capex in the quarter and has repeatedly used asset-backed and contract-backed debt to fund expansion. Its newest $2.6 billion facility carries SOFR plus 5.50%. Higher borrowing costs therefore raise the returns those deployments must ultimately earn for equity holders.

Hedge funds increased CoreWeave while trimming Meta participation

At the end of Q2 2026, Insider Monkey tracked 254 hedge funds holding Meta, down from 262 in Q1. Newlands Management held 9,664,414 shares after a 2% trim. CoreWeave rose to 71 holders from 63, while Magnetar Capital retained 52,062,927 shares after cutting its position 25%. The filings predate September's renewed credit and AI-safety concerns.

At August 31, 55,568,683 CoreWeave shares were sold short, 15.98% of float, with 2.66 days to cover. CoreWeave also had $6.6 billion of 1.75% convertible senior notes outstanding across its 2031 and 2032 issues, so some shorting can reflect capital-structure hedges rather than a simple bearish view.

The $500 billion debt wave matters because it is separating companies that can finance AI from operating cash flow from those that must continuously convince lenders. Meta's main risk is wasting affordable capital. CoreWeave's is paying too much for capital before utilization and margins fully mature. In a slower AI spending cycle, those are very different problems.

Gold is down 1.88% to $4,325.10, and the 10-Year Treasury yield has slipped 0.02% to 4.96%, after reaching 5% for the first time since 2023. Communication stocks and healthcare are leading sector gains, while basic materials and industrials are underperforming.

Today's biggest moves

Meta Platforms is climbing today after Goldman Sachs maintained a Buy rating, stressing the potential upside from its Muse AI agent. Micron Technology tumbled over 5% following warnings about the risks of rapid AI development. Those same concerns drove gains in cybersecurity stocks -- CrowdStrike Holdings soared 15%.

What this means for investors

Tech leaders have issued dire warnings about the risks of rapid artificial intelligence (AI) development in recent days, prompting an industrywide pullback. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman both highlighted the dangers that advanced systems could quickly move beyond human control and called for a slower pace of development.

Investors fear any slowdown could impact demand for AI infrastructure, pressuring some of this year's outperformers, such as Marvell Technology, CoreWeave, and Intel. Those worries are understandable, but it is important think about how any controls on AI development might impact long-term growth. Near-term sentiment may slip, but AI isn't going to disappear, and there is a chance that a slower build-out could actually strengthen the industry in the long term.

title: History Suggests That You'll Regret Not Buying This Struggling Tech Stock
detail:
History Suggests That You'll Regret Not Buying This Struggling Tech Stock
Stefon Walters, The Motley Fool

AAPL

It has been a rollercoaster year for the "Magnificent Seven" stocks, the name given to tech titans Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Tesla, and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META). Of the group, only Meta and Tesla are in the red for the year, down 1.2% and 18.8%, respectively, through market close on Sept. 10.

Both have their fair share of issues, but Meta is a struggling stock that seems to have plenty of upside from its current level. And if history is any indication of what's possible, you may regret not investing while it's having an off year.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Why is Meta's stock struggling?

No single issue is dragging down Meta's stock; it's a combination of factors, with the two main ones being its AI spending and its ongoing regulatory issues.

This year, Meta is slated to spend between $130 billion and $145 billion on AI-related projects, such as building data centers and other infrastructure. In the second quarter (Q2), it spent $31 billion, which, for perspective, is more than all but 26 public companies have made in profits in their past four quarters combined.

Meta's heavy spending weighed on its free cash flow, which fell from $13.2 billion in Q1 to $1.7 billion in Q2. As expected, investors are rarely happy when a company's spending slashes its free cash flow by so much.

META Capital Expenditures (Quarterly) data by YCharts

Regarding regulatory concerns, Meta recently reached a proposed settlement of up to $18 billion due to claims that its apps were purposely addictive and contributed meaningfully to teen mental health decline.

The court case had loomed over Meta for years, and although $18 billion isn't cheap, it's much less than what the company could have faced in a full trial. California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey had sought penalties up to $1.4 trillion. All things considered, Meta has probably never been happier to spend $18 billion.

Can Meta finally start justifying its spending?

One of Meta's first attempts to address investor concerns over its AI spending is the recently announced release of its personal AI agent, Muse.

While companies like ChatGPT's creator, OpenAI, and Claude's creator, Anthropic, have pushed their enterprise and coding tools heavily, Muse is more consumer-focused. Of course, ChatGPT and Claude benefit consumers as well, but Muse is more of a personal assistant for everyday tasks. Meta's stock jumped more than 6% in after-hours trading on Sept. 8 after the release.
